findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Full Year review 2025 26 OSC
findings.headline: Investment income declined 30% year-on-year from £6.4m to £4.5m, driven by falling interest rates.
findings.detail: The council's total investment income for 2025/26 was £4.5m, slightly below the budget of £4.7m. This represents a significant drop from £6.4m in 2024/25, principally because interest rates fell during the year as the Bank of England cut base rate from 4.5% to 3.75%.
findings.matters: Declining investment returns reduce non-tax revenue available to the council and impact its overall financial position; this is a leading indicator of cash yield pressure likely to continue if rates remain low.
findings.figures: 2025/26 actual investment income £4.5m (budget £4.7m), compared to 2024/25 £6.4m; represents 30% year-on-year decline
findings.quote: Total investment income during 2025/26 was £4.5m. This is slightly lower than the £4.7m budget, and considerably lower than the £6.4m return in 2024/25 principally due to the gradual lowering of investment rates

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Full Year review 2025 26 OSC
findings.headline: The council's £5m property fund investment has depreciated by £0.7m to a current valuation of £4.3m, showing market risk on strategic investments.
findings.detail: The Threadneedle Property fund, purchased in 2018 for £5m, has an unrealised loss of £0.7m as at 31 March 2026. The fund returned £210k in dividends (4.2% on original capital) during 2025/26. The council states it does not expect to make new property investments in the near future.
findings.matters: The council's exposure to property market risk and ability to absorb unrealised losses is relevant to its overall financial resilience; the decision to halt new property investments suggests either risk appetite reduction or capital constraints.
findings.figures: Original investment £5m, valuation at 31/03/2026 £4.3m, unrealised loss £0.7m, dividend return £210k (4.2%)
findings.quote: The funds are held with the Threadneedle Property fund, with a valuation of £4.3m which is also £0.7m lower than the original purchase price of £5m.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Full Year review 2025 26 OSC
findings.headline: Three loans made under the council's Investment Strategy have encountered repayment difficulties, totalling £2.7m.
findings.detail: Ethically Sourced Products Ltd's £0.9m loan was due for repayment in 2025/26 and is overdue (working to resolve by early 2026/27). Leicester Community Sports Arena Ltd is currently in arrears on a £1.4m loan. Leicester Hockey Club's £0.4m loan fell into arrears but has now returned to repayment schedule. These represent credit risk on loans made for strategic return purposes.
findings.matters: Lenders assessing the council need to understand its exposure to third-party borrowers and its track record on collecting strategic loans, particularly when borrowers fall behind on obligations.
findings.figures: Ethically Sourced Products Ltd £0.9m (overdue), Leicester Community Sports Arena Ltd £1.4m (in arrears), Leicester Hockey Club £0.4m (previously in arrears, recovered)
findings.quote: Ethically Sourced Products Ltd loan was due for repayment in 2025/26, we are currently working with them to resolve by early 2026/27. Leicester Community Sports Arena Ltd is currently in arrears in relation to the repayment of their loan.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Full Year review 2025 26 OSC
findings.headline: The council is reversing its 2025/26 borrowing strategy in 2026/27, financing £90m of capital from reserves instead of new debt to reduce borrowing costs.
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget moves £90m of previously approved capital expenditure back to reserve financing. This reversal is attributed to 'limited improvements in the financial position' during 2025/26, allowing the council to avoid continued external borrowing and reduce ongoing revenue costs of debt service.
findings.matters: The rapid reversal of strategy signals the underlying cash pressure was temporary or has eased; however, it also indicates reliance on reserves for capital spending rather than sustained operational improvement.
findings.figures: £90 million of capital expenditure reverting from borrowing to reserve financing in 2026/27
findings.quote: However limited improvements in the financial position have allowed this to be reversed in the 2026/27 budget, reducing our borrowing costs going forward.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Full Year review 2025 26 OSC
findings.headline: After 15 years of internal borrowing, Leicester took on £110m in new PWLB debt in 2025/26 to support capital spending and maintain minimum cash balances.
findings.detail: Without external borrowing, the council's cash would have fallen below the £25m minimum threshold by end of 2024/25. They borrowed £110m from PWLB, raising gross debt from £197m to £242m, and maintained cash balances of £62m. This marks a significant break from the council's historical reliance on internal cash reserves.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand why a council abandoned 15 years of cash-funded capital spending and entered the debt markets; this signals underlying cash pressure and changing financial dynamics.
findings.figures: £110m new PWLB borrowing, gross debt increased from £197m (30/09/2025) to £242m (31/03/2026), closing cash balances £62m
findings.quote: During 2025/26 the Council increased its actual borrowing after many years of using internal borrowing as part of its capital financing. This new borrowing totalled £110m from the Public Loans Works Board (PWLB).

findings.headline: Strategic decision to fund £90m of capital from reserves instead of borrowing to reduce future revenue borrowing costs
findings.detail: The Director of Finance has used delegated authority 'to make the most prudent capital financing decisions to support the approach of reducing future borrowing costs to support the budget strategy'. The report notes that £90m of previously approved capital expenditure will be funded from reserves rather than borrowing. This is a deliberate strategy to constrain future borrowing and revenue cost.
findings.matters: While this reduces future debt, it accelerates reserve consumption in the current year. For a lender, this is important: it signals the council is prioritising revenue budget relief over maintaining liquid reserves, which could affect future borrowing capacity if reserves become constrained.
findings.figures: £90m of previously approved capital to be funded from reserves instead of borrowing in 2026-27
findings.quote: The Director of Finance has used their delegation as per the budget strategy 2026/27, to make the most prudent capital financing decisions to support the approach of reducing future borrowing costs to support the budget strategy.

findings.headline: Multiple significant projects on hold pending reviews: SEND places (£6.3m), leisure centres (£1.1m), nursery (£825k) create budget uncertainty
findings.detail: Three substantial capital projects are marked as Purple (on hold): Additional SEND Places is paused 'whilst the total number of SEND places required in the city is confirmed alongside the context of national SEND reforms' (£6.272m); Leisure Centre Improvements are paused 'while the leisure centre review is undertaken' (£1.072m); and Pindar Nursery is on hold 'whilst the requirements for the refurbished building is reviewed' (£825k). These hold uncertain commitments pending external or internal reviews.
findings.matters: Projects on hold tied to external policy changes (SEND reforms, national leisure policy) or internal reviews create budget uncertainty. For a lender, these indicate discretionary spending may be deferred if reviews reach different conclusions.
findings.figures: SEND Places £6.272m, Leisure Centres £1.072m, Pindar Nursery £825k = £8.169m in committed but on-hold budgets
findings.quote: This scheme remains on hold whilst the total number of SEND places required in the city is confirmed alongside the context of national SEND reforms. [Leisure Centre Improvements] This scheme is paused while the leisure centre review is undertaken.

findings.headline: Right to Buy receipts face policy headwind: applications down 40% from peak and further government reforms expected to 'reduce applications and sales in the long-term'
findings.detail: The council received £25.3m in Right to Buy receipts in 2025-26, benefiting from post-November 2024 scheme eligibility changes. However, applications have already dropped 40% from the influx peak, and government announced further reforms in April 2026 including extended eligibility periods and reduced discounts, which the report forecasts will 'further reduce applications and sales in the long-term'.
findings.matters: Right to Buy receipts are discretionary income that can fund capital or be used to offset borrowing. Structural policy headwinds mean this income source is declining. For a lender, this signals shrinking housing capital flexibility.
findings.figures: 2025-26 receipts £25.3m; applications down 40% from peak; government reforms announced April 2026
findings.quote: Applications have since dropped by around 40% compared to historic levels. Government announcements in April 2026 indicate further reforms, including extending the period before which a tenant becomes eligible as well as the discount rules which will further reduce applications and sales in the long-term.

findings.headline: Awaab's Law compliance driving council housing insulation overspend requiring HRA reserve draw
findings.detail: Council Housing Insulation work (budget £200k) has forecast an overspend which the report explicitly attributes to 'Awaab's Law, and the need to respond within prescribed timescales'. The overspend will be funded from HRA reserves. Awaab's Law creates a legal compliance deadline for addressing damp and mould issues in social housing.
findings.matters: This is a regulatory compliance cost driven by a statutory deadline. For a lender, it indicates the council faces legally-mandated spending obligations on housing conditions that cannot be deferred, reducing financial flexibility.
findings.figures: Approved budget £200k; overspend funded from HRA reserves (exact overspend amount not specified)
findings.quote: An overspend has arisen largely as a consequence of Awaab's Law, and the need to respond within prescribed timescales, which will be funded from HRA reserves

findings.headline: £28m of approved capital resources carried forward due to delivery delays, indicating 18.3% slippage against immediate-start budget
findings.detail: Of £161.8m in 'Immediate Starts' capital budgets for 2025-26, only £133.2m was spent. The council approved carry-forward of £28m of slipped resources into 2026-27. Multiple projects report delays due to contractor withdrawal, staffing constraints, procurement delays, and ground condition issues. This systematic slippage suggests delivery capacity constraints.
findings.matters: Large-scale slippage indicates the council may struggle to deliver its capital programme on schedule, which can extend debt service periods and push costs into later years when interest rates may be less favourable.
findings.figures: £28m slippage; total budget £161.8m, spend £133.2m (82% delivery rate)
findings.quote: The progress on spending against work programmes, as shown at Appendix B, and approve the carry-forward of resources into 2026/27 for schemes where spend has slipped (£28m).

findings.headline: Leicester Railway Station Levelling Up project deeply delayed (2.5+ years) with additional funding needed but amount not yet finalised
findings.detail: The £14.2m Leicester Railway Station Levelling Up project was originally scheduled to complete March 2024. As of outturn, completion is marked TBC with procurement not expected to commence until Summer 2026 — a slip of over two years. The report explicitly states the scheme 'is also expected to require additional funding' but 'an exact amount is not yet finalised', creating funding uncertainty on a flagship project.
findings.matters: This is a large, complex scheme (Red rating) with no confirmed completion date and no confirmed additional funding amount. For a lender, this signals major project delivery challenges and unquantified additional borrowing need.
findings.figures: Budget £14.2m; original completion Mar-24, forecast completion TBC; procurement not starting until Summer 2026
findings.quote: The project has been delayed beyond its original completion date, with procurement now expected to commence in Summer 2026. This is a very large and complex scheme and an updated forecast completion date will be provided once more information is known. The scheme is also expected to require additional funding

findings.headline: Leicester Market Redevelopment overspend of £1.9m driven by archaeological findings requires additional funding approval
findings.detail: The Leicester Market Redevelopment project (originally £7.725m budget) has forecast a £1.9m overspend. The overrun is attributed to significant archaeological findings that extended the delivery programme and added costs to the public realm scheme. The report notes that additional funding will be requested but does not confirm the source or timing.
findings.matters: This is a tangible cost overrun on a flagship regeneration project. For a lender, it indicates either scope control weaknesses or unforeseen liabilities emerging mid-project, both of which raise delivery risk on similar schemes.
findings.figures: £1.9m overspend on £7.725m total budget (24.6% overrun); original completion date Dec-21, forecast Dec-26
findings.quote: Significant archaeological fundings have resulted in an extended delivery programme and additional costs associated with the markets public realm scheme. Resulting in a forecast overspend of £1.9m, for which additional funding will be requested in a separate decision report.

findings.headline: Capital receipts target massively missed: £9.9m achieved against £60m budget strategy requirement
findings.detail: The council's budget strategy for 2025-26 required generation of £60m in general fund capital receipts. By end of Q4 2025-26, only £9.9m had been realised. This represents 16.5% of the planned receipts and implies either asset sales are underperforming or the £60m requirement cannot be met, creating a funding gap for planned capital schemes.
findings.matters: Capital receipt shortfalls directly impact available funding for capital programmes. A lender needs to know whether the council has the capacity to fund its committed capital programme or whether it will need to increase borrowing.
findings.figures: £9.9m achieved vs £60m target; represents 16.5% of requirement
findings.quote: To the end of the fourth quarter of 2025/26, the Council has realised £9.9m of General Fund capital receipts.

findings.headline: Reserves position is positive (£71.3m) but highly volatile and dependent on controlling homelessness and social care growth
findings.detail: General reserves available to support 2026-27 and future years stand at £71.3m. However, the report explicitly warns this projection is 'highly volatile', with a multiplicative effect: a £15m per-year increase in homelessness and social care pressures would deplete reserves by £45m over the medium term. Reserves are the buffer, not a solution.
findings.matters: While the current reserve position looks adequate, the council recognises it is not resilient to sustained demand pressure. A lender needs to understand that reserves are being drawn down to fund service gaps and will erode unless structural pressures are addressed.
findings.figures: £71.3m reserves available for 2026-27 and future budgets, £194m available at start of 2025-26
findings.quote: Members are asked to note that this projection is highly volatile, and the forecast of reserves is even more volatile than assumptions about income and expenditure due to the multiplicative effect

findings.headline: BIFFA waste contract dispute settled for £10m; contracted through 2029 with indexation risk
findings.detail: A protracted commercial dispute on the BIFFA Leicester waste contract (in place since 2003, valued at £405m over its lifetime) was settled by payment of £10m after mediation. This is less than 2.5% of total contract value but represents a one-off cost absorbed in 2025-26. The contract has inflation indexation, so future costs depend on waste volumes and price escalation.
findings.matters: This shows the council faced a significant unplanned commercial liability. Future waste costs are locked in by contract but exposed to inflation and volume changes.
findings.figures: £10m settlement, £405m total contract value over lifetime, contract in place since 2003
findings.quote: a protracted commercial dispute arose that was eventually settled with a payment to BIFFA of £10m after mediation, less than 2.5% of the contract value.

findings.headline: Staffing vacancies are masking underlying service deficits and may not be sustainable
findings.detail: The council's ability to stay within overall budget relies heavily on unfilled posts across multiple departments. Adult Social Care underspent by £1.7m partly due to vacancies; Children's Services by £3.7m due to social worker and educational psychologist vacancies. While recruitment efforts continue (including international recruitment), this is a temporary saving that disappears as vacancies fill.
findings.matters: Vacancy-driven underspends are transient. They mask service delivery issues and statutory responsibilities. When posts are filled (which they will be), this £5-6m in underspends reverses into overspends.
findings.figures: Approximately £1.7m vacancy underspend in Adult Social Care, £3.7m in Education & Children's Services
findings.quote: Approximately £1.7m of the underspend is as a result of vacancies throughout the year. There have been difficulties recruiting to social worker posts, as well as recruiting to commissioning teams.

findings.headline: Looked-after children placement costs overspent by £2.1m due to rising numbers and complex cases
findings.detail: Placement costs within children's services overspent by £2.1m. Numbers of children in care rose to 717 from 643 last year, and a small number of expensive complex cases pushed costs higher. The council is planning to build two new children's homes (opening 2027), partly funded by the Department of Education, to manage costs.
findings.matters: This is demand-led growth: a rising number of children entering care, a demographic and safeguarding trend that drives costs. The council has limited control over the intake and must fund placements.
findings.figures: £2.1m overspend on placement costs, 717 children in care episode during year (up from 643)
findings.quote: Placement costs within children have a pressure of £2.1m, due to an increase in numbers and the complexity cases.

findings.headline: Housing benefit subsidy shortfall of £4.1m driven by supported accommodation rents exceeding government maxima
findings.detail: The council faces a net shortfall on housing benefit subsidy of £4.1m. This arises because rents for supported accommodation can be significantly higher than the maximum subsidy the government will pay. The council must fund the gap. This is a persistent structural issue, not a one-off.
findings.matters: This is a recurring budget pressure with no solution. It represents an implicit subsidy to supported accommodation residents that the council must absorb from general funds.
findings.figures: £4.1m net shortfall on housing benefit subsidy in 2025-26
findings.quote: we continue to see a net shortfall on housing benefit subsidy of £4.1m. This largely relates to supported accommodation where rents can be significantly higher than the maximum amount of subsidy paid by the government.

findings.headline: Savings targets are only 75% achieved with £4.9m still to find by 2027-28
findings.detail: The council set a savings target of £19.5m by 2027-28 (down from an original £23m). To date only £14.6m has been achieved. Outstanding savings of £4.9m remain to be identified and delivered. The report notes that some original targets were found to be unrealistic.
findings.matters: The council's budget strategy depends on sustained savings delivery. Being behind on this track record suggests the remaining £4.9m may also slip, creating a structural deficit.
findings.figures: £14.6m achieved of £19.5m target (75%), £4.9m outstanding by 2027-28
findings.quote: Whilst £9.7m of the £12.3m in-year savings target has been achieved to date, continued focus will be required to ensure outstanding targets of £4.9m are achieved by 2027/28.

findings.headline: DSG deficit reached £37.9m but hinges on government approval of a SEND reform plan
findings.detail: The cumulative Dedicated Schools Grant deficit has grown to £37.9m. The Government has committed to fund 90% of the 2025-26 accrual, but this is conditional on Leicester submitting and gaining approval of a SEND reform plan. Support is forecast to continue for two more years (2027-28, 2028-29), saving the council £0.6m in 2026-27 borrowing costs rising to £1.2m in 2027-28.
findings.matters: This is a critical dependency on government policy and plan approval. Any delay or non-approval reverses the funding benefit. The in-year high needs overspend was £18.9m this year alone.
findings.figures: £37.9m cumulative deficit, Government funding 90% of 2025-26 accrual, saves £0.6m 2026-27 and £1.2m 2027-28 in borrowing costs
findings.quote: The cumulative Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) deficit has increased to £37.9m at 31 March 2026. Whilst the deficit remains a significant financial issue, the Government has confirmed within the 2026/27 settlement that it will fund 90% of the deficit accrued to 2025/26, significantly reducing the financial impact on the Council.

findings.headline: Homelessness costs consumed £4.5m of contingency with no permanent funding solution in sight
findings.detail: Homelessness used £4.5m of corporate contingency and increased £0.9m since period 9. Without the £45m investment in temporary accommodation, costs would have been £20m higher this year. The ongoing pressure reflects a national issue: presentation demand continues to rise while grant funding and housing benefit are insufficient.
findings.matters: This is a structural, demand-driven deficit that grows with economic conditions. Lenders need to know the council's homelessness spend is dependent on sustained discretionary investment, not grant funding.
findings.figures: £4.5m used from contingency in 2025-26, £0.9m increase from period 9, would have been £20m higher without £45m temporary accommodation investment
findings.quote: Homelessness required £4.5m of the contingency, this is a £0.9m increase from period 9. However, we must remember this cost was forecast to have been £20m higher if it had not been for the £45m investment in temporary accommodation.

findings.headline: Awaab's Law compliance adds £2.098m in new unavoidable regulatory costs with ongoing impact
findings.detail: The council must implement Awaab's Law (effective 27 October 2025), which requires investigation and remediation of emergency and significant damp and mould hazards within strict timeframes. This accounts for £2.098m of the £6.244m total cost pressures identified. The council plans to complete damp and mould work on 2,900 properties in 2026/27, with ongoing remediation required in future years.
findings.matters: New regulatory requirements are consuming budget capacity and will continue to do so, leaving no room for cost overruns given the thin reserves position. Compliance failures could trigger regulatory intervention and reputational damage.
findings.figures: £2.098m in legislative and regulatory pressures; 2,900 properties requiring damp/mould remediation in 2026/27
findings.quote: There is a pressure arising from the need to create additional capacity and resource in relation to the implementation of Awaab's Law, alongside the continued roll out of Electrical Installation Condition Reports (EICR's).

findings.headline: Right to Buy generating £1.1m income loss in 2026/27 from surge of applications before discount reduction
findings.detail: Applications surged before the November 2024 reduction in the RTB discount threshold (from £102,400 to £24,000). These are still being processed, generating an estimated £1.1m income loss in 2026/27. While the lower discount should help long-term finances, the council acknowledges that 'economies of scale that come from managing a large portfolio are gradually being eroded' as stock reduces. 146 homes were lost to RTB in 2024/25.
findings.matters: RTB creates both near-term income loss and long-term structural erosion of the HRA's asset base and cost efficiency, creating ongoing pressure that cannot be recovered through higher rents and reduces future debt serviceability.
findings.figures: £1.094m RTB cost pressure; 146 homes lost in 2024/25; discount reduced from £102,400 to £24,000 from Nov 2024
findings.quote: As a result, it is predicted that the HRA will suffer an income loss of £1.1m in 2026/27 from sales under Right to Buy.

findings.headline: Budget balance depends entirely on achieving the full 4.8% rent increase; any shortfall creates a deficit
findings.detail: The council states that applying a rent increase below 4.8% would trigger a budget shortfall requiring either capital programme cuts, reserve drawdowns, or service reductions. The revenue impact is £1m for each 1% increase foregone in 2026/27 alone, and £11.1m over ten years. This leaves the council with zero flexibility in its core income assumptions.
findings.matters: If rent collection weakens due to tenant hardship, or if the council faces political pressure to moderate increases, the HRA would immediately fall into deficit with only £0.5m reserves to absorb it. This also constrains governance decisions.
findings.figures: Loss of over £1m per 1% below 4.8% in 2026/27; £11.1m cumulative loss over 10 years if 2.5% applied instead of 4.8%
findings.quote: Applying a rent increase below 4.8% would lead to a budget shortfall, and further work would be required to bridge this gap; if, for example, a 2.5% increase was to be applied then this would lead to a £2m shortfall in the budget.

findings.headline: Unallocated HRA reserves critically low at only £0.5m against £313m debt and structural financial risks
findings.detail: The council will hold only £0.5m in unallocated reserves at 1 April 2026. The council explicitly flags this as concerning: 'a very small sum, particularly given the short and medium-term financial risks facing the HRA.' The remaining £17.3m of total reserves are fully committed (£5m minimum working balances, £7.7m for prior capital approvals, £4.6m earmarked for anticipated costs).
findings.matters: Very thin reserves leave the HRA with minimal buffer to absorb any budget shocks, overspends, or income shortfalls, and significantly constrain borrowing capacity for new investment.
findings.figures: Opening reserves £17.8m; unallocated £0.5m; committed: £5.0m minimum balances + £7.7m prior approvals + £4.6m earmarked
findings.quote: Forecast Opening Reserves Balance as at 1st April 2026 £17.8m... Forecast Unallocated Reserves Balance as at 31st March 2027 £0.5m. This is a very small sum, particularly given the short and medium-term financial risks facing the HRA.

findings.headline: Waste contract reset in May 2028 expected to cost £3m more per year
findings.detail: The council has received provisional Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) funding of £7.4m for 2026/27 for waste packaging, but 'we have only limited information about likely levels of income in later years, which will depend on producers' responses to the new levy'. Separately, the waste PFI contract resets in May 2028, and the council expects waste costs to increase 'up to £3m per year' from this alone. This is a known cliff-edge cost that will hit the budget beyond the current three-year strategy.
findings.matters: A material, known cost increase (£3m/year) appears in budget forecasts but is not yet built into savings plans beyond 2028/29. The EPR funding is also uncertain in future years, creating a potential income cliff if producers reduce use of packaged goods.
findings.figures: EPR funding £7.4m in 2026/27, future years uncertain; waste contract cost increase up to £3m per year from May 2028
findings.quote: we expect waste costs to increase by up to £3m per year when there is a new contract in May 2028. We have only limited information about likely levels of income in later years, which will depend on producers' responses to the new levy.

findings.headline: DSG deficit government support is contingent on SEND reform plan approval and covers only 90%
findings.detail: The council had provisionally planned to set aside reserves for a £44.8m DSG deficit forecast by end of 2025/26. Government announced unexpectedly that they would cover 90%, expected to save the council £0.6m in 2026/27 rising to £1.2m in 2027/28. However, this support is 'subject to approval of the local SEND reform plan' and only covers to March 2026. The council must still fund 10% locally (£4.5m set aside in 2026/27, £2.7m in 2027/28). Beyond 2028, deficits become central government's responsibility.
findings.matters: The council is dependent on a government commitment that is (a) conditional on a plan it must produce, (b) only covers to 2028 after which central government takes the deficit, and (c) still requires 10% local funding each year. The underlying SEND cost growth is unresolved and the council's ability to influence it is unclear.
findings.figures: DSG deficit forecast £44.8m by end 2025/26; government covers 90%; council sets aside £4.5m in 2026/27, £2.7m in 2027/28, £2.8m in 2028/29 for remaining 10%; support conditional on SEND reform plan approval
findings.quote: they will provide grant funding to cover 90% of the cumulative deficit to March 2026, and has strongly implied that funding will also be available for the next two years. It should be noted that this is subject to approval of the local SEND reform plan. The remaining deficit will have to be funded locally.

findings.headline: Business rates pool dissolved, removing £6m+ per year of supplementary funding
findings.detail: The council has historically retained over £6m per year from a rates pool shared with Leicestershire authorities. The rates reset and changes to the rates retention system have made this pool 'unviable in 2026/27' and authorities have agreed to disband it. This is a permanent loss of income with no stated replacement.
findings.matters: This is a £6m+ permanent reduction in funding from a source the council has relied on and that required cooperation with other councils to maintain. It represents loss of discretionary surplus funding at a time the council is claiming to have stabilised.
findings.figures: Over £6m per year historic supplementary funding from rates pool
findings.quote: Under the previous business retention arrangements, a "rates pool" across Leicester and Leicestershire allowed a greater share of rates to be retained locally, and shared across the pool authorities. This has served us well: over recent years, our share of the additional rates has been over £6m per year... The rates reset, and other changes to the rates retention system, make the pool unviable in 2026/27 and the authorities involved have agreed to disband it.

findings.headline: Homelessness numbers rising despite £45m temporary accommodation investment
findings.detail: The council budgeted £11m growth plus £6m contingency in 2025/26 for homelessness. Investment of £45m in temporary accommodation is claimed to have avoided £50m of costs by 2026/27. However, the paper explicitly states 'the number of cases continues to increase and (without further action) will put further pressure on future years' budgets'. The council is now proposing an additional £50m capital for property acquisitions and additional staffing.
findings.matters: A lender sees this as cost containment that is not containing costs: investment is rising, mitigation is claimed but the underlying driver (presentation rate) is still accelerating. The council describes homelessness budget as 'under severe pressure', and each cycle requires new capital investment to avoid blowing the revenue budget.
findings.figures: £11m growth, £6m contingency in 2025/26; £45m investment claimed to avoid £50m costs; additional £50m capital now proposed; revenue impact £1.9m in 2026/27, £4.2m in 2027/28
findings.quote: the number of cases continues to increase and (without further action) will put further pressure on future years' budgets.

findings.headline: Adult social care cost trajectory grown by £37m over three years despite ongoing control work
findings.detail: Adult social care is forecast to grow from £179.3m (underlying budget) to £216.3m by 2028/29. The council claims its cost-mitigation work prevented £24m of overspend in 2025/26 (rising to £41m in 2026/27), but even with this control in place, costs will increase by almost £40m over the strategy period. The service was also rated 'Requires Improvement' by the CQC in July 2025, triggering an action plan.
findings.matters: Adult social care is the largest spending pressure on councils and the CQC finding signals governance or service-quality issues. The gap between what mitigation 'saves' (£24-41m) and what growth still occurs (£40m total) suggests mitigation work is running on a treadmill and not solving the underlying driver (demographic growth + wage inflation on contracted care).
findings.figures: £179.3m to £216.3m growth; £24m prevented in 2025/26; £41m prevented in 2026/27; CQC Requires Improvement, July 2025
findings.quote: the department may have spent £24m more in 2025/26 (rising to £41m in 2026/27) if cost mitigation work had not taken place. This programme of work continues, and the future growth pressures identified above takes this into account. Despite this work, it is forecast that costs of care will increase by almost £40m over the three years of this strategy.

findings.headline: Savings programme cannot deliver original targets
findings.detail: The council approved £23m of savings in February 2025 but now acknowledges £3.3m of those targets are 'not realistically achievable'. Estates & Building Services £0.8m, Neighbourhoods £0.5m, Corporate Services £1.1m, and Finance £0.9m of the planned savings have been withdrawn. By period 6 2025/26, only 70% of revised targets had been achieved, leaving a shortfall to deliver in the second half of the year.
findings.matters: A council cannot borrow its way out of missed savings targets, and unachievable programmes indicate either planning failure or service-delivery constraints that recur. This leaves less room for absorbed cost growth.
findings.figures: £23m target reduced to £19.5m; £3.3m of reductions; 70% achieved to date against revised total
findings.quote: Since the original target was set, it has become clear that some targets are not realistically achievable. The figures in this report therefore reflect a reduced target of £19.5m by 2027/28.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy Report Updated Feb26
findings.headline: Investment income will decline in coming years as interest rates fall and investment balances are managed down
findings.detail: The council expects Bank of England base rate cuts to continue in early 2026/27. As base rates fall, returns on the council's cash investments will decline significantly. The council also expects to reduce total investment balances over time to minimise the need for borrowing, further reducing investment income available to the revenue budget.
findings.matters: Investment income is a secondary revenue source for councils. A sustained decline in investment yields, combined with shrinking investment balances, reduces this income stream at a time when the council is managing cash depletion and rising debt service costs.
findings.figures: Bank of England base rate at 3.75% (May, August, December 2025 cuts of 25bps each); rate expected to fall further in early 2026/27
findings.quote: It is likely that interest earned on investments will decrease over the next few years as balances to invest is managed to minimise the need to borrow and interest rates gradually decrease.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy Report Updated Feb26
findings.headline: Property fund investments have underperformed since 2018, sustaining capital losses
findings.detail: The council has £4.33m currently invested in property funds (of a £30m permitted limit). The document explicitly states performance has been disappointing since these investments were made in 2018, with capital losses occurring, though income has so far outweighed the losses. The council now states it has no current intention to invest new funds into property funds.
findings.matters: Underperforming pooled investments indicate either poor timing, poor selection, or deteriorating property market conditions. The admission to avoid new property fund investment suggests the council is retreating from this asset class due to poor returns.
findings.figures: £4.33m currently invested of £30m limit; invested since 2018 (8 years of disappointing performance)
findings.quote: Performance has been disappointing since we invested in these funds in 2018, though the capital losses have been outweighed by the income received to date. There is no current intention to invest new funds into property funds.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy Report Updated Feb26
findings.headline: Council has shifted from maintaining cash reserves to regular prudential borrowing for capital spending
findings.detail: The council had not needed to borrow for several years prior to 2024/25 because it held healthy cash balances. This changed as earmarked capital resources were spent and reserves depleted. The council is now borrowing regularly through the PWLB to fund the capital programme, a material shift in funding strategy.
findings.matters: A move from self-funded capital spending to external borrowing increases the council's debt burden and interest costs, and indicates reserves are being consumed faster than they can be replenished. Lenders track reserve depletion as a risk indicator.
findings.figures: Cash balances fell to around £50m at end of 2024/25; external debt forecast to rise from £174m (actual 31/03/2025) to £256m (estimated average 2028/29); total investments expected around £100m in 2025/26 and 2026/27
findings.quote: Prior to 2024/25 the Council had maintained healthy cash balances and had not needed to borrow for several years. This position has now shifted as reserves and cash balances have been reduced and the council has borrowed to fund the capital programme.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Feb26 Final Capital Budget Report - Council 250226 AO
findings.headline: Homelessness approaches have increased 219% since 2014/15, outpacing council's acquisition capacity
findings.detail: Number of households approaching homelessness teams for advice and support has grown from 2,163 in 2014/15 to 6,891 in 2024/25. As of October 2025, 1,100 households remain in temporary accommodation. Despite prevention performance better than national average (59% vs 51%), demand continues to exceed the council's ability to house via council-owned stock.
findings.matters: Structural demand growth in a core service (homelessness) that the council is managing through capital investment and revenue subsidy, indicating a service pressure that capital spending alone cannot resolve and which will continue to generate revenue cost pressure.
findings.figures: 219% increase in approaches 2014/15 to 2024/25 (2,163 to 6,891); 1,100 currently in TA; prevention duty outcome 59% (vs 51% national average)
findings.quote: Since 2014/15 the number of approaches has risen by 219%... As of October 2025, we had a total of 1,100 households residing in temporary accommodation.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Feb26 Final Capital Budget Report - Council 250226 AO
findings.headline: Council explicitly states it is in a 'parlous financial position' requiring prudential borrowing as budget strategy
findings.detail: Within the capital strategy section on financing, the council states that due to financial difficulty, prudential borrowing is now a structural part of the budget strategy rather than an exception. This is a direct acknowledgment of constrained finances that drives capital financing decisions.
findings.matters: Explicit statement of financial stress indicates the council is not in a comfortable financial position; borrowing strategy is driven by constraint rather than opportunity, raising questions about sustainability of the £82.54m prudential borrowing programme.
findings.figures: £82.54m prudential borrowing proposed; maximum revenue impact 2026/27 £3.3m, 2027/28 £6.2m, 2028/29 £7.1m
findings.quote: Due to the parlous financial position we are in, prudential borrowing is part of our Budget Strategy. Capital spending proposals will consequently only be approved in the light of the revenue implications.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Feb26 Final Capital Budget Report - Council 250226 AO
findings.headline: £50m temporary accommodation acquisition programme driven by revenue cost control, with demand forecast to exceed supply
findings.detail: Council investing £50m (following £45m in March 2024) to acquire 250 temporary accommodation units (90 singles, 160 families). Forecast cost avoidance is £3.8m in 2026/27 rising to £6.4m in 2027/28. However, 452 families and 261 singles are still expected to remain in expensive temporary accommodation by March 2027 despite this investment, indicating the demand problem outpaces the capital solution.
findings.matters: Capital programme is being used to manage revenue costs rather than deliver strategic assets; ongoing demand for homelessness services exceeds the council's capacity to address it through acquisitions alone, indicating a structural service pressure.
findings.figures: £50m capital; 90 singles units + 160 family units; 452 families and 261 singles forecast in expensive TA by March 2027; cost avoidance £3.8m (2026/27) and £6.4m (2027/28)
findings.quote: The proposed capital budget provides an additional £50m for acquiring temporary accommodation during 2026/27. This is anticipated to provide 90 units for singles and 160 units for families... it is expected that numbers will continue to exceed LCC owned and commissioned temporary accommodation with 392 families in expensive temporary accommodation and 81 singles in expensive temporary accommodation as at March 2026. These figures are expected to grow to 452 families and 261 singles in expensive temporary accommodation by March 2027

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Feb26 Final Capital Budget Report - Council 250226 AO
findings.headline: £90m of previously approved capital spending now funded from reserves instead of borrowing
findings.detail: The council has switched from funding capital via capital receipts and the capital fund to using borrowing; now reverting to fund £90m from reserves to reduce ongoing revenue borrowing costs. An additional £60m in capital receipts will be used to further reduce the need to borrow. This indicates the council is drawing down reserves to manage the capital programme rather than financing it through sustainable sources.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion constrains future financing flexibility and suggests the council is managing within tight revenue constraints rather than having structural capacity for the capital programme.
findings.figures: £90m from reserves; £60m capital receipts to reduce borrowing
findings.quote: it is proposed within the Revenue budget report (also included in the agenda) to fund £90m of previously approved capital expenditure from reserves instead of borrowing, and therefore reducing the ongoing revenue borrowing costs incurred

findings.paper_title: Leicester City Council Interim Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25 - 25 November 2025
findings.headline: Council underspent by £15.4m in 2024/25 and has delivered 65% of multi-year savings target, showing progress on cost control
findings.detail: Against background of significant challenges, the council delivered a £15.4m underspend in 2024/25, mainly in Adult Social Care (£5.4m) and Education/Children's Services (£6.5m). Reduced reserves usage from £61m planned to £21.6m actual. Cumulative savings achieved to date: £5.8m (2025/26), £9m (2026/27), £9.5m (2027/28). As of April-June 2025/26, £15m of £23m (65%) of near-term savings target achieved.
findings.matters: Demonstrates the council has genuine capacity to identify and deliver cost reductions, which is essential if it is to bridge its forecast gaps. Track record matters to lenders assessing financial sustainability.
findings.figures: 2024/25 underspend: £15.4m. Cumulative savings: £5.8m (2025/26), £9m (2026/27), £9.5m (2027/28). 2025/26 YTD: £15m of £23m savings target (65%) achieved by June 2025.
findings.quote: For 2024/25 the Council has made considerable progress in reducing its cost and managing demand in key service areas. This enabled the Council to reduce the use of reserves in 2024/25 from £61.0m to £21.6m.

findings.paper_title: Leicester City Council Interim Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25 - 25 November 2025
findings.headline: Council does not publicly report on performance against key strategic priorities
findings.detail: The auditor found no evidence that corporate performance reports on operational, workforce or finance metrics are prepared and presented regularly. Performance is reported only to individual scrutiny commissions but not consolidated or published. No formal approach exists to ensure data quality in performance reporting.
findings.matters: Lack of public performance reporting against strategic objectives weakens accountability and decision-making transparency. Lenders need visibility of whether a council is delivering against its strategic plan and managing operational risks.
findings.figures: No corporate performance reports found in publicly available meeting documentation.
findings.quote: Our review of publicly available meeting documentation did not evidence that corporate performance reports detailing operational services, workforce and finance are prepared and presented on a regular basis.

findings.paper_title: Leicester City Council Interim Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25 - 25 November 2025
findings.headline: Errors in draft accounts and failure to implement IFRS 16 (major accounting standard) delayed audit completion
findings.detail: The council's draft accounts contained errors requiring additional audit work. Critically, the council did not account for IFRS 16 (lease accounting standard) which came into effect 1 April 2024. Management's work on this area was ongoing at time of report writing, extending audit completion beyond the statutory deadline. An unqualified opinion is now anticipated in December 2025.
findings.matters: Errors in accounts preparation and late implementation of mandatory accounting standards indicate control weakness in the finance function and risk of material misstatement. Lenders rely on timely, accurate financial reporting.
findings.figures: Audit completion delayed; IFRS 16 implementation work ongoing at time of interim report (August 2025).
findings.quote: Our audit work has identified errors in the draft financial statements, which has led to additional work and extended testing. We have also experienced delays to the completion of the audit due to the Council's draft accounts not accounting for the implementation of IFRS 16, which came into effect 1 April 2024.

findings.paper_title: Leicester City Council Interim Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25 - 25 November 2025
findings.headline: Housing regulator gave council C3 rating ('serious failings and significant improvement needed') with 70% of stock lacking electrical safety tests
findings.detail: In July 2025, the Regulator of Social Housing inspected the council's housing properties and issued a C3 consumer standards rating. Key failures: 70% of properties had not had an electrical safety test; last comprehensive hazard survey was 2009; weakness in repairs and maintenance service; concerns over complaints handling. The council received 52% of all complaints over 12 months relating to housing. The council disputes the harshness of the judgement but acknowledges the issues.
findings.matters: This signals major operational and reputational failure in a material council service. Safety failures expose the council to legal liability and tenant dissatisfaction. The scale of backlog (70% without electrical testing) indicates systemic control weakness in a large asset base.
findings.figures: 70% of properties without electrical safety test. Last comprehensive hazard survey: 2009 (16-year gap). Housing complaints: 52% of all council complaints over 12-month period.
findings.quote: Issues found included: 70% of properties owned by the Council had not had an electrical safety test at the time of the visit. The Council was unable to evidence the properties were free of category one hazards as the last comprehensive survey took place in 2009.

findings.paper_title: Leicester City Council Interim Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25 - 25 November 2025
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit forecasts to reach £45m by March 2026, eating into reserves
findings.detail: The cumulative DSG deficit reached £22.2m at 31 March 2025, with an in-year deficit of £12.6m in 2024/25. The council forecasts this will reach £45m by 31 March 2026. While government has extended a statutory override allowing treatment as a negative reserve until 31 March 2028, the ongoing overspending drains council finances and reduces interest earned on balances or increases borrowing costs.
findings.matters: The DSG deficit represents statutory education spending the council cannot refuse. It directly reduces the council's available resources for other services and borrowing capacity, and signals inability to manage high-needs SEND placements within budget.
findings.figures: DSG deficit: £6.0m (March 2023), £9.6m (March 2024), £22.2m (March 2025). In-year deficit 2024/25: £12.6m. Forecast cumulative deficit: £45m by 31 March 2026.
findings.quote: The DSG deficit was £6.0m at 31 March 2023 and £9.6m at 31 March 2024. The in-year deficit for 2024/25 was £12.6m, taking the cumulative deficit to £22.2m. The Council forecasts that this will rise to £45m by 31 March 2026.

findings.paper_title: Leicester City Council Interim Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25 - 25 November 2025
findings.headline: Recurring budget gaps of £30-68m over three years with reserves depleting to only 6% of budget
findings.detail: The council faces recurring budget gaps of £30.1m in 2025/26, £46.2m in 2026/27 and £68.1m in 2027/28, which it plans to meet from reserves. Reserves will fall to £25.2m (around 6% of the 2025/26 budget of £405m) by end-2025/26, leaving only one year of cover for the forecast overspending. The council remains dependent on one-off items including £90m of capital reserves being used for revenue expenditure.
findings.matters: Lenders need to know if a council can continue to service debt and fund services. Reserve depletion below prudent levels signals immediate financial stress and loss of shock-absorption capacity.
findings.figures: Recurring gaps: £30.1m (2025/26); £46.2m (2026/27); £68.1m (2027/28). Reserves: £25.2m projected at end 2025/26 (6% of budget). Current reserves £103.8m projected to £55m by end 2027/28.
findings.quote: Considerable additional savings will still be required, with recurring budget gaps of £30.1m in 2025/26; £46.2m in 2026/27 and £68.1m in 2027/28 which would be met from reserves. Reserves would fall to £25.2m, which is around 6% of the 2025/26 budget

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Mid year Treasury report CMB Final Version 211125 AO
findings.headline: Threadneedle Property Fund investment showing £0.67m unrealised loss since 2018
findings.detail: The council's £5m investment in Threadneedle Property Fund made in 2018 has depreciated to £4.33m as of September 2025, representing a £0.67m unrealised loss, though the overall position including £1.55m in interest received shows a net gain of £0.88m.
findings.matters: Demonstrates the council is exposed to property market asset price volatility through its investment strategy, with material loss potential in stressed market conditions.
findings.figures: Initial investment £5m, current value £4.33m, unrealised loss £0.67m, interest received £1.55m
findings.quote: Council has invested £5m in the Threadneedle Property Fund Trust since 2018. At the 30 September 2025 this fund had a value of £4.3m.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Mid year Treasury report CMB Final Version 211125 AO
findings.headline: Council's treasury investments have declined £48m year-on-year, falling from £157.7m to £109.7m
findings.detail: While investments increased from £51.8m at 31 March 2025 to £109.7m by 30 September 2025, this still represents a significant £48m decline compared to the September 2024 position. Though some seasonal variation is normal, the longer-term trend shows sustained pressure on cash reserves.
findings.matters: Demonstrates the council's cash position is under sustained downward pressure, limiting financial flexibility and explaining why external borrowing has become necessary.
findings.figures: £109.7m at 30 September 2025, £48m below September 2024 position, £51.8m at 31 March 2025
findings.quote: It should be noted though that this is £48m less than the position in September 2024.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Mid year Treasury report CMB Final Version 211125 AO
findings.headline: Council has borrowed £40m in July 2025 after more than a decade without taking on new external debt
findings.detail: After more than 10 years of not borrowing, Leicester City Council took out £40m in July 2025 and is planning additional borrowing in October and early 2026. This shift was driven by reduced cash balances and increased need to fund the capital programme through external borrowing rather than internal reserves.
findings.matters: Shows the council's accumulated cash reserves have depleted to the point it can no longer fund capital spending internally, forcing a return to external borrowing and introducing interest rate and refinancing risk.
findings.figures: £40m borrowed in July 2025, gross debt increased from £173.6m (31 March 2025) to £216.2m (30 September 2025) at average interest rate of 4.4%
findings.quote: Up until last year the Council had not borrowed for over a decade. However, as cash balances have reduced this period and the increased need to fund the capital programme with borrowing, the Council is once again utilising government borrowing facilities.

news_drafts.headline: Investment income declined 30% year-on-year from £6.4m to £4.5m, driven by falling interest rates.
news_drafts.lead: Declining investment returns reduce non-tax revenue available to the council and impact its overall financial position; this is a leading indicator of cash yield pressure likely to continue if rates remain low.
news_drafts.paper_title: Treasury Management Full Year review 2025 26 OSC

news_drafts.headline: The council's £5m property fund investment has depreciated by £0.7m to a current valuation of £4.3m, showing market risk on strategic investments.
news_drafts.lead: The council's exposure to property market risk and ability to absorb unrealised losses is relevant to its overall financial resilience; the decision to halt new property investments suggests either risk appetite reduction or capital constraints.
news_drafts.paper_title: Treasury Management Full Year review 2025 26 OSC

news_drafts.headline: Three loans made under the council's Investment Strategy have encountered repayment difficulties, totalling £2.7m.
news_drafts.lead: Lenders assessing the council need to understand its exposure to third-party borrowers and its track record on collecting strategic loans, particularly when borrowers fall behind on obligations.
news_drafts.paper_title: Treasury Management Full Year review 2025 26 OSC
